paragraphs: This paper studies robustness by asking how changes to underlying causes produce changes in observed inputs. Its scope includes both classification and more general measurement data. The central idea is to represent possible input manipulations within a causal model, so that the model explicitly accounts for how those manipulations affect what it observes.

The resulting system, deep CAMA, models manipulations of selected causes and their consequences for observed effects. The authors also develop data augmentation and fine-tuning at test time to improve its robustness. These methods accompany the causal representation, giving the approach both a way to describe manipulations and training or adaptation procedures intended to handle them.

In the reported comparison, deep CAMA is more robust to previously unseen manipulations than discriminative deep neural networks. It also learns representations that separate manipulation-related information from other hidden causes. This separation is a useful additional result: the learned representation distinguishes factors associated with manipulation from other factors contributing to the observation.
neurips-2020-a-causal-view-on-robustness.tldr: Deep CAMA explicitly models causal manipulations and shows improved robustness to unseen manipulations while separating their representations from other latent causes.

paragraphs: Modern meta-learning often trains on episodes with separate support and query data. This strategy is widely believed to help a learner generalize to test environments. The paper examines that belief theoretically, focusing on how the training strategy influences a generalization bound rather than treating episodic training as an unexplained design choice.

Using a stability perspective, the authors analyze generic meta-learning algorithms trained with support/query episodes. They obtain a bound of order 1/√n, where n is the number of tasks. Its notable feature is that it does not depend on m, the number of samples within each task. This describes the dependence of the bound; it does not say that within-task data can never affect actual performance.

Under the common few-shot assumption that m is much smaller than n, the result supplies strong generalization guarantees. The authors also propose leave-one-out training to investigate how changing the training strategy affects generalization. Experiments using popular meta-learning algorithms on standard few-shot regression and classification tasks support their analysis.
neurips-2020-a-closer-look-at-the-traini.tldr: A stability analysis gives support/query meta-learning a generalization bound depending on the number of tasks rather than samples per task.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for training predictive models that approximately meet the equalized odds fairness criterion. It addresses both how to encourage the criterion during learning and how to evaluate a fitted model afterward. These are distinct tasks: a training objective can encourage fairness, while a statistical test assesses evidence of a violation.

The authors introduce a differentiable discrepancy measure that quantifies departures from equalized odds. Adding this measure as a penalty steers model parameters toward the criterion. Both training and testing use a resampled version of the sensitive attribute that satisfies equalized odds by construction, providing a common basis for the two procedures.

The evaluation component is a formal hypothesis test for violations, described as the first such test in the literature. Demonstrations cover regression and multiclass classification and report improved performance over existing leading methods. The framework also incorporates uncertainty quantification that is unbiased for each studied group, allowing reported analytical results to include group-equitable uncertainty information.
neurips-2020-achieving-equalized-odds-by.tldr: Resampling sensitive attributes supports both a differentiable equalized odds training penalty and a formal test for fairness violations.

paragraphs: The paper considers streaming algorithms whose input can be selected maliciously by an adaptive adversary. The desired property is adversarial robustness: the algorithm should retain its accuracy guarantees even in this setting. The challenge therefore concerns the reliability of the algorithm when the process supplying its data can adapt, rather than assuming an input stream chosen independently of that process.

The authors establish a connection between this robustness requirement and differential privacy. They use the connection to construct new streaming algorithms with adversarial robustness. Differential privacy thus serves as a tool for obtaining accuracy guarantees under adaptive input selection, giving the work a role beyond the privacy setting suggested by its terminology.

The resulting algorithms outperform the strongest existing constructions in many parameter regimes. That qualification matters: the stated improvement applies across many regimes, rather than being asserted for every possible parameter choice. The contribution combines a conceptual connection between two research problems with algorithmic improvements derived from that connection.
neurips-2020-adversarially-robust-stream.tldr: A connection to differential privacy yields adversarially robust streaming algorithms that improve on existing constructions in many parameter regimes.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse concerns recommending actions that change an algorithmic decision. Such recommendations need to account for causal relationships between features, yet the equations governing those relationships are generally unknown. The authors first show that guaranteed recourse is impossible without access to the true structural equations, motivating recommendations that explicitly account for uncertainty.

They develop two probabilistic approaches for choosing actions that achieve recourse with high probability under limited causal knowledge. The first assumes additive Gaussian noise and uses Bayesian model averaging to represent uncertainty over structural equations and estimate counterfactual outcomes. It therefore incorporates uncertainty into predictions about what would happen to the individual after an action.

The second avoids assumptions about the structural equations by changing the target: it estimates average intervention effects for people similar to the individual seeking recourse. This yields a subpopulation-based notion of recourse rather than the same individual counterfactual quantity. A gradient-based procedure selects actions, and experiments find more reliable recommendations than non-probabilistic baselines when causal knowledge is imperfect.
neurips-2020-algorithmic-recourse-under-.tldr: Two probabilistic recourse methods account for imperfect causal knowledge and empirically provide more reliable action recommendations than non-probabilistic baselines.

paragraphs: Neural text generation faces a tension between dependencies among output words and parallel computation. Fully autoregressive models generate through serial decoding, while non-autoregressive approaches can decode in parallel without output dependencies. This paper proposes an autoregressive approach whose parallel generation time grows sublinearly, aiming to retain useful dependencies while reducing sequential work.

The approach builds on the observation that conditional random fields with bounded context can be decoded in parallel. The authors organize generation into a decoding cascade and introduce the Markov transformer to parameterize it. This transformer variant supports simultaneous decoding with specified cutoffs on autoregressive context, making the amount of available context part of the decoding design.

Training requires only a small change to standard autoregressive training. On five machine translation datasets, the method demonstrates a competitive tradeoff between accuracy and speed relative to existing approaches. The stated finding concerns that tradeoff: the cascade provides a way to combine dependent outputs with faster parallel generation while maintaining competitive translation quality.
neurips-2020-cascaded-text-generation-wi.tldr: Markov transformers use bounded-context cascaded decoding to achieve sublinear parallel generation time with a competitive translation accuracy–speed tradeoff.

paragraphs: Panel data track multiple individuals over multiple time periods. The paper develops coresets for regression in this setting: much smaller datasets designed to approximate the relevant regression problem. Previous coreset results covered either many individuals at a single time or one individual over many times, leaving the combined panel setting unaddressed.

The authors define coresets for several panel regression variants and give efficient construction algorithms. Their coreset sizes are independent of both the number of individuals and the number of time periods. Instead, size depends polynomially on the number of regression parameters and the inverse of the allowed error, connecting the required summary size to model complexity and approximation accuracy.

The construction uses the Feldman–Langberg framework and bounds total sensitivity, roughly the aggregate maximum influence of individual-time observations across parameter choices. Tests on synthetic and real-world data produce coresets much smaller than the full datasets and speed up evaluation of the regression objective. These findings support the computational value of the theoretical size guarantees.
neurips-2020-coresets-for-regressions-wi.tldr: The paper constructs panel-regression coresets whose sizes do not depend on the number of individuals or time periods.

paragraphs: Measurements of a physical system may capture only a few channels, leaving important dynamical variables hidden. Many methods for learning latent dynamics instead assume observations have more intrinsic dimensions than the underlying system. This paper studies the opposite situation: recovering hidden governing coordinates from a time series with relatively few measured dimensions.

Inspired by classical methods for partially observed chaotic attractors, the authors introduce an embedding technique for both single-variable and multivariable time series. It uses an autoencoder trained with a new loss in the latent space. The aim is to obtain a representation of the underlying dynamics from observations that do not directly reveal all of their coordinates.

The technique reconstructs strange attractors from synthetic and real systems better than existing methods in the reported comparisons. It also produces consistent, predictive representations for stochastic systems. Applications include patient electrocardiograms, household electricity use, neural spikes, and Old Faithful eruptions, illustrating its use for exploring dynamical structure across different kinds of measured time series.
neurips-2020-deep-reconstruction-of-stra.tldr: An autoencoder with a new latent-space loss reconstructs hidden dynamical attractors from low-dimensional time series.

paragraphs: This paper addresses contextual bandit learning when actions range over a continuous space and the structure of that space is unknown. The central objective is computational tractability: the authors seek a learning procedure that can work in this setting while remaining feasible to compute. Continuous actions are a defining part of the problem being addressed.

The proposed algorithm uses a reduction-based design and can be combined with most supervised learning representations. This compatibility matters because the bandit method can work with a broad range of representations used for supervised learning. The contribution therefore includes both an algorithm for the continuous-action setting and a way to connect it to existing representation choices.

The authors provide a general theoretical result supporting the algorithm and verify its new functionality through large-scale experiments. The theory and experiments supply complementary evidence: one supports the method analytically, while the other demonstrates it in empirical use. Together, the stated results establish a computationally tractable approach with broad representational compatibility.
neurips-2020-efficient-contextual-bandit.tldr: A tractable reduction-based algorithm handles contextual bandits with continuous actions and works with most supervised learning representations.

paragraphs: The paper studies functions formed by adding a small number of complex exponential terms, each with its own coefficient and frequency. It proves explicit upper bounds on their leverage scores under Gaussian and Laplace measures. These results extend earlier bounds for the uniform measure and provide mathematical tools for choosing informative samples or features.

One application is a new random Fourier features algorithm for approximating Gaussian and Cauchy kernel matrices. For low-dimensional data, it uses a nearly optimal number of features and runs in time polynomial in the matrix's statistical dimension. The authors establish this property for an oblivious sketching method beyond the previously covered polynomial kernel, resolving an open question.

A second application uses the bounds to construct nonuniform sampling distributions for robust active learning with Gaussian- or Laplace-distributed data. Within an existing framework, the authors obtain essentially optimal results for bandlimited interpolation, multiband interpolation, and Gaussian process regression. The significance is that these sampling guarantees extend beyond the uniform-data setting covered by earlier work.
neurips-2020-fourier-sparse-leverage-sco.tldr: New Fourier-sparse leverage-score bounds enable efficient kernel approximations and essentially optimal active-learning results for Gaussian and Laplace data.

paragraphs: Requirements such as nonnegativity, monotonicity, and convexity can improve interpretability and often help when data are scarce. Enforcing them as hard constraints is difficult, however. Earlier approaches commonly use soft penalties, transformations tailored to particular cases, or restricted function families. The paper investigates how to enforce such requirements within flexible kernel machines.

The authors prove that hard affine constraints on function derivatives can be encoded in this setting. They develop a tightened reformulation using second-order cone constraints, allowing the resulting optimization problem to be implemented in convex solvers. This links mathematical shape requirements to a concrete optimization formulation rather than leaving them as preferences in the learning objective.

The paper also proves performance guarantees for the resulting solution. Demonstrations include joint quantile regression, with applications to economics and aircraft trajectory analysis among others. The contribution is a method for combining kernel-based flexibility with formally enforced derivative constraints, together with theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence of the approach's efficiency.
neurips-2020-hard-shape-constrained-kern.tldr: A convex optimization reformulation lets kernel machines enforce hard affine derivative constraints with performance guarantees.

paragraphs: In deterministic actor–critic control, the actor improves its actions using the critic's gradient with respect to those actions. Yet critics are typically trained to predict expected returns. The paper highlights a mismatch: the quantity used to update the policy is an action gradient, while the usual training target concerns the value itself.

The proposed MAGE algorithm explicitly learns the action-value gradient. It uses a learned dynamics model and backpropagates through that model to construct gradient targets for temporal-difference learning. Grounded in policy-gradient theory, this procedure trains the critic around the information that the actor needs for policy improvement, making the critic's learning objective more directly aligned with its role.

The authors evaluate MAGE on a set of MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and demonstrate its efficiency relative to leading model-free and model-based baselines. The empirical result supports the usefulness of targeting action gradients in these tasks. The central contribution is the combination of learned dynamics and gradient-targeted critic training for deterministic policy optimization.
neurips-2020-how-to-learn-a-useful-criti.tldr: MAGE trains critics explicitly on action-value gradients using learned dynamics, improving their usefulness for continuous-control policy optimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated set selection when the reward function is revealed only after each choice. At every round, an algorithm chooses a feasible set and then an adversary supplies a nonnegative submodular function. The objective is to control expected approximate regret, measuring performance against a comparator with an approximation allowance.

The authors develop a general approach using first-order regret bounds from online linear optimization. For monotone functions under a matroid constraint, they obtain a regret bound of order √(kT ln(n/k)) at approximation level 1 − c/e − ε. Here n is the ground-set size, k the matroid rank, T the number of rounds, and c the average curvature. The result improves earlier bounds even when c is set to one.

For nonmonotone functions without constraints, the algorithm achieves half-approximation regret of order √(nT), also improving prior results. The approach uses Blackwell approachability and establishes a new first-order bound for the instances arising here. The common contribution is sharper online guarantees across two different submodular maximization settings.
neurips-2020-improved-algorithms-for-onl.tldr: First-order regret analysis yields improved online guarantees for both matroid-constrained monotone and unconstrained nonmonotone submodular maximization.

paragraphs: Box embeddings represent objects as multidimensional rectangles. Containment naturally represents transitive asymmetric relationships, while intersections and easily computed volumes support probabilistic representations. These useful geometric properties also create a learning problem: whole neighborhoods of parameter values can produce the same loss, leaving optimization unable to distinguish nearby alternatives.

Earlier work addressed some of this local identifiability problem through an approximation to Gaussian convolution over box parameters, but its intersection operation also made gradients sparser. This paper instead models box parameters using minimum and maximum Gumbel distributions. The distributions are chosen so that intersecting boxes preserves the relevant family, retaining a key structural property of the representation.

With this construction, the expected intersection volume depends on all parameters. That provides a route for the learning objective to involve parameters that could otherwise receive little useful gradient information. Experiments demonstrate a drastic improvement in the models' ability to learn. The result connects the choice of probabilistic box parameterization directly to better optimization behavior.
neurips-2020-improving-local-identifiabi.tldr: Gumbel-distributed box parameters preserve intersection structure while making expected intersection volumes involve all parameters, substantially improving learning experimentally.

paragraphs: Metamaterials obtain complex large-scale behavior from modular internal structures. Simulating those structures can require detailed finite element meshes, making the governing partial differential equations expensive to solve. This paper uses the modular structure to learn component-level approximations that can be assembled into a cheaper model of the full material.

A neural network predicts a component's stored potential energy from its boundary conditions. The component models are then composed, and the material's macroscopic behavior is determined by minimizing the approximate total potential energy. This formulation reduces simulation to variables on component boundaries while retaining an energy-based relationship between the components and the full structure.

Training examples come from finite element analyses of individual components, avoiding costly ground-truth simulations of the complete structure for that purpose. Dataset aggregation guides the selection of training data so that the component models work accurately when combined. The reported result is accurate macroscopic behavior from the composed surrogates and accelerated simulation of parametric metamaterials.
neurips-2020-learning-composable-energy-.tldr: Neural component-energy models compose into reduced simulations that accurately reproduce macroscopic metamaterial behavior while accelerating computation.

paragraphs: Classification ultimately seeks a low probability of making an incorrect prediction, expressed by expected zero-one loss. Conventional learning methods typically optimize a surrogate loss within a selected family of classification rules. This paper introduces minimax risk classifiers that avoid relying on those choices and directly address worst-case expected zero-one loss.

The method considers uncertainty sets of distributions defined through linear constraints. These sets include the true underlying distribution, and learning minimizes the worst expected classification loss over the set. The uncertainty set therefore plays a central role: it specifies which distributions the classifier must account for when choosing a rule.

Training also provides tight lower and upper bounds on expected zero-one loss, giving performance guarantees alongside the learned classifier. The authors derive finite-sample generalization bounds involving training-set size and the smallest minimax risk. On benchmark datasets, the classifiers perform competitively with leading techniques. The contribution combines direct treatment of classification error, distributional uncertainty, and explicit performance bounds.
neurips-2020-minimax-classification-with.tldr: Minimax risk classifiers optimize worst-case zero-one loss over distributional uncertainty sets and provide tight performance bounds during learning.

paragraphs: Collision avoidance becomes difficult when robots face uncertain measurements, uncertain motion, and incomplete information. This paper develops a method that accounts for both measurement and motion uncertainty. Its objective is to identify admissible control actions with formally supported probabilistic safety, allowing uncertainty to enter the collision-avoidance calculation explicitly.

The authors introduce Probabilistic Safety Barrier Certificates based on Control Barrier Functions. These certificates convert a chance-constrained safety set into deterministic constraints on control actions. A quadratic program then finds an alternative controller that satisfies the certificate constraints while making the smallest required modification to an existing controller.

The approach requires uncertainty to have finite support but does not impose additional assumptions on its form. Within that setting, it also enables worst-case guarantees. Experiments in realistic simulation environments demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution links probabilistic safety requirements to an implementable controller adjustment, while retaining the stated finite-support condition behind its treatment of uncertainty.
neurips-2020-multi-robot-collision-avoid.tldr: Probabilistic safety certificates turn collision-avoidance requirements into controller constraints under measurement and motion uncertainty with finite support.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose a high-quality item while satisfying differential privacy. The input consists of a finite collection of candidates and a quality score for each. The objective is to return an item with as large a score as possible while respecting the privacy requirement governing the selection mechanism.

The authors propose Permute-and-Flip as an alternative to the commonly used exponential mechanism. Its design comes from a careful analysis of the privacy constraints. The key result compares expected scores: the new mechanism's expectation is always at least as large as that of the exponential mechanism. This guarantee concerns average selection quality under the mechanism's randomness.

The improvement can reach a factor of two, although that maximum gain is not asserted for every input. The method is also simple to implement and runs in time linear in the number of candidates. These properties pair a strong expected-quality comparison with a computationally straightforward mechanism for private selection.
neurips-2020-permute-and-flip-a-new-mech.tldr: Permute-and-Flip performs private selection in linear time with expected score at least as high as the exponential mechanism.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a continuous-time counterpart of stochastic gradient descent for two-layer neural networks as the hidden layer becomes arbitrarily wide. It treats the dynamics as an interacting particle system and asks how the behavior of individual particles relates to a limiting description of the network as a whole.

The authors establish propagation of chaos under different scenarios: statistical interactions between particles vanish asymptotically. They quantify how individual particles converge, as the number of neurons increases, toward a solution of a mean-field McKean–Vlasov equation. Wasserstein distance supplies the measure of convergence, making the result quantitative rather than only identifying a limiting equation.

The analysis allows SGD step sizes to depend on both network width and iteration number. It identifies two regimes with different mean-field limits, one corresponding to an implicitly regularized optimization problem. Experiments on real classification datasets support the existence of these regimes and illustrate the convergence results. The work shows that step-size scaling can affect which limiting training behavior emerges.
neurips-2020-quantitative-propagation-of.tldr: A quantitative mean-field analysis of wide-network training identifies two step-size regimes, including one with implicit regularization.

paragraphs: The paper develops a distribution-comparison approach for generative adversarial learning. It starts from GAN variants that use integral probability metrics to improve stability and reduce mode collapse, interpreting these as comparisons of moments in a critic's embedded space. The proposed generalization uses characteristic functions, which uniquely encode a distribution's information.

The authors establish interpretations of characteristic-function phase and amplitude and use these to provide a way of balancing generation accuracy and diversity. They also develop an efficient sampling strategy for calculating characteristic functions. A further theoretical result establishes equivalence between comparisons in the embedded and data domains when a reciprocal exists, making that condition central to the claimed equivalence.

The resulting reciprocal characteristic-function GAN uses an autoencoder structure with two modules and a simple training strategy. Comparisons take place in the embedded space, while the model supports generation and reconstruction. Experiments report superior performance on both tasks. The contribution connects distribution comparison, a conditional domain-equivalence result, and a compact bidirectional generative architecture.
neurips-2020-reciprocal-adversarial-lear.tldr: RCF-GAN compares characteristic functions in an embedded space and reports improved generation and reconstruction using a two-module autoencoder structure.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor prediction relies on retaining training data, which becomes difficult when datasets are large or spread across locations and times. This paper analyzes distributed nearest-neighbor classification as a way to address that obstacle. The central question is how combining predictions from subsamples affects statistical accuracy compared with an oracle version.

With majority voting, the distributed classifier achieves the oracle's convergence rate in regret, up to a multiplicative constant depending only on data dimension. Replacing majority voting with weighted voting eliminates that multiplicative difference. The aggregation rule therefore matters even when both approaches attain the same broad convergence-rate behavior.

The authors also derive sharp upper bounds on how many subsamples can be used while preserving the optimal convergence rate. Weighted voting permits more subsamples than majority voting under these bounds. Numerical studies support the theoretical findings. The results explain both the statistical cost of distribution and how weighted aggregation allows a greater degree of splitting without losing the optimal rate.
neurips-2020-statistical-guarantees-of-d.tldr: Weighted voting removes an oracle-comparison penalty in distributed nearest-neighbor classification and permits more subsamples while retaining optimal convergence.

paragraphs: The paper addresses sampling from difficult distributions known only up to a normalization factor. It builds on Langevin dynamics, where successive samples can be strongly correlated. The proposed change uses previous trajectories to encourage more diverse samples, with the aim of obtaining more useful information from the sampling process.

The authors introduce a repulsive force based on the Stein variational gradient that pushes samples away from past trajectories. They report substantially reduced autocorrelation and a corresponding increase in effective sample size. Crucially, their theoretical analysis establishes that the asymptotic stationary distribution remains correct despite adding this force, owing to the special properties of the Stein gradient.

Extensive empirical studies show much higher sampling efficiency and better uncertainty estimation than ordinary Langevin dynamics. The theoretical and empirical results address different aspects of the method: preserving the desired distribution in the long run and improving the usefulness of generated samples in practice. Together, they support using sampling history to reduce redundant exploration.
neurips-2020-stein-self-repulsive-dynami.tldr: A Stein-based repulsive force reduces Langevin sample autocorrelation while preserving the correct asymptotic stationary distribution.

paragraphs: Synbols is a tool for creating synthetic image datasets that probe particular properties and failure modes of learning algorithms. Its motivation is that benchmark design influences what researchers can discover about a method. Being able to construct a dataset around a specific question makes that dataset an instrument for examining algorithm behavior.

The tool renders low-resolution images using Unicode symbols and artistic fonts from the open font community. Its high-level interface allows users to specify distributions over the underlying features that produce an image, including textures and occlusions. This makes it possible to vary the composition of generated data while working through a common dataset-generation interface.

The authors demonstrate Synbols across supervised learning, active learning, generalization outside the training distribution, unsupervised representation learning, and object counting. In these settings, they use generated datasets to examine limitations and flaws in standard algorithms. The contribution is both a practical generator and a demonstration that controlled synthetic data can support targeted investigation across several learning problems.
neurips-2020-synbols-probing-learning-al.tldr: Synbols generates controllable synthetic symbol images for investigating learning algorithms' properties and failure modes.

paragraphs: This paper examines how stopping optimization early can provide statistical control without adding an explicit regularization term. Its setting is unconstrained mirror descent applied to unregularized empirical squared loss for linear models and kernel methods. The quantity of interest is excess risk, which captures the statistical quality of the learned prediction rule.

The authors complete an inequality associated with convexity of squared loss and use it to connect offset Rademacher complexity with potential-based analysis of mirror descent. This links a statistical measure of function-class complexity to the analysis of optimization progress. The connection yields guarantees along the sequence of iterates, rather than only describing a final optimized solution.

The relevant function classes depend on the mirror map, initialization, step size, and number of iterations. These choices therefore enter the resulting excess-risk guarantees and explain how the optimization path contributes to implicit regularization. The theory recovers several recent results through short proofs and improves some of them in particular settings, providing a unified route to analyzing early stopping.
neurips-2020-the-statistical-complexity-.tldr: A link between statistical complexity and mirror-descent convergence yields excess-risk guarantees for early-stopped linear and kernel learning.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering research often improves recommendation accuracy through more elaborate models or additional information. This paper instead examines the input ratings themselves. It proposes a data-debugging framework that identifies overly personalized ratings whose presence hurts the performance of a particular collaborative filtering model, making the data distribution an explicit target for improvement.

The framework searches for a small collection of ratings whose modification or deletion would produce a nearly optimal improvement in validation-set recommendation accuracy. This ties the choice of edits to their effect on the model's measured performance. The selected ratings are therefore identified in relation to the model and validation objective used by the framework.

Experiments show significant accuracy improvements. The authors also observe that selected ratings differ substantially from their items' average ratings and that the method tends to move them toward those averages. This finding exposes a tension in the optimization objective: improving overall accuracy can favor reducing strongly individualized signals. The paper uses that observation to inform the balance between recommendation accuracy and personalization.
neurips-2020-trading-personalization-for.tldr: Editing a small set of influential ratings improves collaborative-filtering accuracy while revealing a tradeoff with personalization.
